claim: IR60b is expressed in the labral sense organ (LSO) in sensillum 7 of the Drosophila pharynx.
source: IR60b is expressed in the LSO in sensillum 7 (Figure 1A–C), which houses eight neurons (Gendre et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data shown in Figure 1C and stated in the text.

claim: IR60b is the only member of the IR20a clade showing a significantly negative Direction of Selection (DoS) signature.
source: IR60b is unique among the genes of this IR clade in showing the signature of purifying selection (Figure 1D) (Koh et al., 2014; Mackay et al., 2012; Stoletzki and Eyre-Walker, 2011), suggesting that IR60b represents a particularly effective solution to a difficult evolutionary problem.
evidence: The claim is supported by DoS analysis shown in Figure 1D and cited references.

claim: IR60b is expressed in a neuron distinct from those expressing Gr64a.
source: We found that while IR60b-GAL4 labels a single neuron in the LSO (Figure 2A; the arrowhead indicates a labeled cell body in one of the two bilaterally symmetric neurons), and Gr64a-GAL4 labels two neurons (Figure 2B), together the two drivers label three neurons (Figure 2C). The simplest interpretation of these results is that IR60b is expressed in a neuron distinct from those that express Gr64a.
evidence: The claim is supported by double-driver expression analysis shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: IR60b is expressed in a neuron distinct from those expressing Gr43a.
source: Similar analysis with the Gr43a-GAL4 driver confirmed this conclusion (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by double-driver expression analysis shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: IR60b co-expresses with IR94f in the same neuron.
source: Although the IR60b driver did not coexpress with any of these Gr drivers, it did coexpress with IR94f-GAL4 (Figure 2J–L)
evidence: The claim is supported by double-driver expression analysis shown in Figure 2J-L.

claim: IR60b co-expresses with IR94h in the same neuron.
source: Although the IR60b driver did not coexpress with any of these Gr drivers, it did coexpress with IR94f-GAL4 (Figure 2J–L) and IR94h-GAL4 (Figure 2M–O).
evidence: The claim is supported by double-driver expression analysis shown in Figure 2M-O.

claim: Silencing of the IR60b neuron increases sucrose feeding time.
source: Surprisingly, silencing of IR60b neurons caused a robust increase in feeding time when flies were tested with 300 mM sucrose (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data using tetanus toxin to silence neurons, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Silencing of the IR60b neuron increases feeding time across a broad range of sucrose concentrations.
source: We confirmed and extended this finding by testing across a broad range of sucrose concentrations. At all sucrose concentrations, the silenced flies showed greater feeding times than the parental controls, which were equivalent to each other (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response behavioral data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Silencing of the IR60b neuron does not affect pumping rate.
source: The silencing of the IR60b neuron did not affect pumping rate at any concentration (Figure 4C), arguing that increased feeding times were not due to motor defects that caused flies to swallow at a lower rate.
evidence: The claim is supported by pumping rate measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Silencing of the IR60b neuron does not affect feeding on glucose, fructose, or trehalose at 300 mM.
source: We tested 300 mM concentrations of fructose, trehalose, and glucose, and found no effects of silencing (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data testing multiple sugars shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Optogenetic activation of the IR60b neuron decreases trehalose feeding.
source: We found that optogenetic activation of the IR60b neuron with red light reduced trehalose feeding of IR60b-GAL4/UAS-Chrimson flies (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic activation experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The IR60b1 mutant shows increased feeding time when tested with 300 mM sucrose.
source: The IR60b1 mutant showed a robust increase in feeding time when tested with 300 mM sucrose (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from CRISPR-generated mutant shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The IR60b1 mutation is recessive.
source: The homozygous IR60b1/IR60b1mutant showed a much greater feeding time than either the parental control or an IR60b1/+ heterozygote. The heterozygote showed the same phenotype as the control, supporting the interpretation that the phenotype is due to a recessive mutation in IR60b.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of homozygous and heterozygous mutant phenotypes.

claim: The IR60b1 mutant shows increased feeding time across a broad range of sucrose concentrations.
source: We confirmed and extended these results by testing a broad range of sucrose concentrations (Figure 5B). At all sucrose concentrations, the mutant showed greater feeding times than the controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response behavioral data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The IR60b2 mutant shows increased feeding time similar to IR60b1.
source: As a further confirmation of the requirement for IR60b, we tested an independent allele, IR60b2, which was generated and backcrossed using the same protocol as for IR60b1. This second allele produced an increase in feeding time very similar to that of IR60b1 (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from a second independent mutant allele shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The IR60b1 mutant consumes a greater volume of sucrose than control flies.
source: We found that not only was the mean feeding time greater for the mutant than the control (Figure 5E), but the volume ingested was greater as well (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by volume measurements from individual flies shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: The IR60b1 mutant and control flies show the same linear relationship between feeding time and volume consumed.
source: The mutant and control flies showed the same linear relationship between feeding time and volume consumed; the slopes were statistically indistinguishable, consistent with an equivalent feeding rate (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Among nine sugars tested, only sucrose elicited increased feeding in the IR60b1 mutant at 100 mM and 300 mM concentrations.
source: Only sucrose, among the nine sugars tested, elicited increased feeding in the IR60b1 mutant at concentrations of either 100 mM or 300 mM (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral testing with a panel of sugars shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: At 900 mM concentration, sucrose and glucose elicited increased feeding in the IR60b1 mutant.
source: At 900 mM concentrations, sucrose and glucose elicited increased feeding (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data at high sugar concentrations shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The IR60b1 mutation does not affect responses to bitter compounds (caffeine, coumarin, lobeline).
source: We tested a series of concentrations of three bitter compounds: caffeine, coumarin, and lobeline, and found that in wild type all three reduce mean trehalose feeding time, in a dose-dependent fashion (Figure 6D). The extent of reduction was not affected by the IR60b mutation.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral testing with bitter compounds shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The IR60b1 mutation does not affect feeding responses to NaCl or KCl.
source: We found no effect of IR60b1 on the feeding time elicited by a range of NaCl or KCl concentrations (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral testing with salts shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The IR60b1 mutation does not affect feeding responses to pH variations.
source: Nor was there an effect on feeding at a range of pH values.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral testing with pH variations.

claim: The IR60b1 mutation does not affect feeding responses to amino acids.
source: Finally, we tested several amino acids and found no effect of IR60b1 (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral testing with amino acids shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Sucrose elicits an increase in Ca2+ levels in IR60b neurons.
source: We found that a sucrose stimulus elicited an increase in fluorescence in IR60b neurons, indicating an increase in Ca2+ levels (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Water does not elicit an increase in Ca2+ levels in IR60b neurons.
source: A control water stimulus did not elicit such an increase, indicating that the response is not due to mechanosensory stimulation (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging control experiments shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The Ca2+ response in IR60b neurons to sucrose takes approximately 30 seconds to reach peak amplitude.
source: Once the stimulus perfuses through the system to the neuron and the Ca2+ response becomes detectable, it takes on the order of 30 s to reach peak amplitude (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7D,E.

claim: Among five stimuli tested, the IR60b neuron was activated only by sucrose and glucose at 900 mM.
source: Consistent with these results, of five stimuli tested in parallel, the IR60b neuron was activated only by sucrose and glucose, each tested at 900 mM (Figure 7F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging with multiple stimuli shown in Figure 7F,G.

claim: The sucrose response of the IR60b neuron is dependent on IR60b.
source: Finally, we asked whether the sucrose response of the IR60b neuron was dependent on IR60b. We used IR60b-GAL4 to express GCaMP6s in an IR60b1 background and, in parallel, in a control background. Both these genotypes contained a single copy of the IR60b-GAL4 driver, whereas the flies in our earlier imaging experiments contained two copies and thus presumably higher levels of GCaMP6s. Nonetheless, sucrose elicited a clear Ca2+ signal in the control background. The signal was essentially eliminated in the IR60b1 mutant background (Figure 7H).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging in mutant background shown in Figure 7H.

claim: IR60b1 mutant flies show three times longer contact time with sucrose than controls in the FLIC assay.
source: Strikingly, IR60b1 mutants made contact with sucrose for three times longer than controls during this period (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIC assay data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: IR60b1 mutants approach food wells and make contact the same number of times as controls.
source: IR60b1 mutants approached the wells and made contact with the food the same number of times as the control (Figure 8D), as if locomotion and foraging capabilities are unaffected by the mutation.
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIC assay data on contact frequency shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The mean duration of individual contact events is longer in IR60b1 mutants than controls.
source: However, the mean duration of individual contact events was longer in the IR60b1 (Figure 8E–G), thereby accounting for the greater overall contact time.
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIC assay data on contact duration shown in Figure 8E-G.

claim: IR60b acts to limit the duration of individual feeding bouts.
source: IR60b acts to limit the duration of individual feeding bouts.
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIC assay data showing longer contact durations in mutants.

claim: The Drosophila taste system has many parallels to that of mammals.
source: The initiation of feeding has been studied in the model genetic system Drosophila, whose taste system has many parallels to that of mammals (Liman et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Liman et al., 2014.

claim: Discrete classes of taste receptors and neurons assess the molecular composition of a potential food source in Drosophila.
source: A variety of molecular and cellular mechanisms must operate for feeding to be initiated. Discrete classes of taste receptors and neurons assess the molecular composition of a potential food source (Marella et al., 2006; Thorne et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Marella et al., 2006 and Thorne et al., 2004.

claim: Receptors sensitive to sugars signal the presence of nutrients in Drosophila.
source: Receptors sensitive to sugars signal the presence of nutrients (Dahanukar et al., 2007; Freeman et al., 2014; Jiao et al., 2008; Wisotsky et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Receptors sensitive to bitter-tasting compounds signal the danger of toxins in Drosophila.
source: receptors sensitive to bitter-tasting compounds signal the danger of toxins (Lee et al., 2009, 2015; Shim et al., 2015; Weiss et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The termination of feeding, once begun, is poorly understood.
source: The termination of feeding, once begun, is poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Previously described mechanisms that terminate feeding are based in central neural circuits that act downstream from taste neurons.
source: Previously described mechanisms that terminate feeding are based in central neural circuits that act downstream from taste neurons (Hergarden et al., 2012; Pool et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hergarden et al., 2012 and Pool et al., 2014.

claim: Some feeding termination mechanisms involve internal sensors that monitor post-ingestive nutrient concentrations in the hemolymph.
source: Some involve internal sensors that monitor post-ingestive nutrient concentrations in the hemolymph (Dus et al., 2015; Miyamoto et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dus et al., 2015 and Miyamoto et al., 2012.

claim: Some feeding termination mechanisms involve internal sensors that monitor mechanical tension in the gut.
source: Some involve internal sensors that monitor post-ingestive nutrient concentrations in the hemolymph (Dus et al., 2015; Miyamoto et al., 2012) or mechanical tension in the gut (Olds and Xu, 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Olds and Xu, 2014.

claim: Some feeding termination mechanisms involve cells in the taste center of the brain that are controlled by the satiety state of the fly.
source: while others involve cells in the taste center of the brain that are controlled by the satiety state of the fly (Marella et al., 2012; Yapici et al., 2016; Zhan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Marella et al., 2012, Yapici et al., 2016, and Zhan et al., 2016.

claim: The gustatory organs of the fly include the legs, the labellum, and the pharyngeal sense organs.
source: The gustatory organs of the fly include the legs, the labellum, and the pharyngeal sense organs, which include the labral sense organ (LSO)(Gendre et al., 2004; Stocker, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gendre et al., 2004 and Stocker, 1994.

claim: Taste reception in Drosophila gustatory organs is mediated by Gustatory receptors (Grs).
source: Taste reception in these organs is mediated by a large number of receptors, including those of the Gustatory receptor (Gr) family (Clyne et al., 2000; Scott et al., 2001), which detect a variety of sugars and bitter compounds (Liman et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Clyne et al., 2000, Scott et al., 2001, and Liman et al., 2014.

claim: Members of the ionotropic receptor (IR) family are expressed in taste organs.
source: Members of an ancient class of sensory receptors called the ionotropic receptors (IRs) were recently found be expressed in taste organs (Benton et al., 2009; Croset et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Benton et al., 2009 and Croset et al., 2010.

claim: A large clade of IRs called the IR20a clade are mapped to taste neurons in the legs, labellum, and pharynx.
source: In particular, a large clade of IRs called the IR20a clade were mapped to taste neurons in the legs, labellum, and pharynx (Koh et al., 2014; Stewart et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Koh et al., 2014 and Stewart et al., 2015.

claim: Two IR20a clade genes expressed in the male leg have roles in male mating behavior, presumably as pheromone receptors.
source: The functions of the IR20a clade genes are virtually unexplored, although analysis of two that are expressed in the male leg has revealed roles in male mating behavior, presumably as pheromone receptors (Koh et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Koh et al., 2014.

claim: Sensillum 7 of the LSO houses eight neurons.
source: IR60b is expressed in the LSO in sensillum 7 (Figure 1A–C), which houses eight neurons (Gendre et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gendre et al., 2004.

claim: Two neurons in sensillum 7 coexpress Gr43a, Gr61a, Gr64a, Gr64e, and Gr64f and promote consumption of sweet foods.
source: Two of these neurons have been shown to coexpress a set of sugar-sensing Gr-GAL4 or Gr-LexA drivers, including drivers of Gr43a, Gr61a, Gr64a, Gr64e, and Gr64f (LeDue et al., 2015). These two neurons promote the consumption of sweet foods.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to LeDue et al., 2015.

claim: Six neurons in sensillum 7 have not been assigned a molecular identity and their function is unknown.
source: The other six neurons have not been assigned a molecular identity, and their function is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge regarding these neurons.

claim: The total time of feeding increases with sucrose concentration and saturates at approximately 100 mM.
source: We verified that flies exhibit robust consumption of sucrose solutions in this paradigm across a wide range of concentrations (Figure 3C). The total time of feeding increased with sucrose concentration and saturated at ~100 mM.
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The rate of pumping is independent of sucrose concentration below 1M.
source: The rate of pumping in this paradigm, that is the swallowing rate, was independent of concentration (Figure 3D), consistent with previous results that pumping rate is not impeded by viscosity at sucrose concentrations less than 1M (Manzo et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by pumping rate data shown in Figure 3D and citation to Manzo et al., 2012.

claim: The presence of blue dye does not affect feeding behavior in the pharyngeal pumping assay.
source: To facilitate analysis of food consumption by direct visual inspection, we added a blue dye to the food samples. Control experiments indicated that the presence of the dye did not affect the results (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Flies consume approximately 8 nanoliters per second in the pharyngeal pumping assay.
source: Flies consumed ~8 nanoliters/s, which is comparable to reported values (Qi et al., 2015; Yapici et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by volume measurements and citations to Qi et al., 2015 and Yapici et al., 2016.

claim: Silencing IR94f neurons increases sucrose feeding time.
source: To confirm the role of the IR60b neuron, we used an independent driver, IR94f-GAL4, which we had found to be coexpressed with IR60b-GAL4 in the same neuron (Figure 2L). We confirmed with this driver that silencing the neuron increased the intake of the sucrose source (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data using IR94f-GAL4 driver shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The IR60b1 mutation lacks 66% of the IR60b coding sequence.
source: To test the hypothesis that the IR60b receptor functions in the limitation of sucrose feeding, we used CRISPR-Cas9 to create a mutant allele that lacks 66% of the IR60b coding sequence (Gratz et al., 2014) (Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by description of the CRISPR-generated mutation and citation to Gratz et al., 2014.

claim: The IR60b1 mutation eliminates all three predicted transmembrane domains of IR60b.
source: The mutation was designed to eliminate all three of the predicted three transmembrane domains of IR60b.
evidence: The claim describes the design of the mutation.

claim: The rise time of the Ca2+ response in IR60b neurons is comparable to that observed for some tastants in pharyngeal neurons of the larval taste system.
source: This rise time is comparable to that observed for some tastants in pharyngeal neurons of the larval taste system (Apostolopoulou et al., 2016; Choi et al., 2016; van Giesen et al., 2016b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Apostolopoulou et al., 2016, Choi et al., 2016, and van Giesen et al., 2016b.

claim: The rise time of the Gr43a neuron response to sugar is faster than that of the IR60b neuron.
source: However, the rise time of the Gr43a neuron, once it begins to respond to sugar, is faster (LeDue et al., 2015), suggesting that the Gr43a neuron activates a circuit that stimulates feeding before the IR60b neuron activates a circuit that inhibits feeding.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to LeDue et al., 2015 and inference about circuit dynamics.

claim: IR94f-GAL4 driven GCaMP6s shows a Ca2+ response to sucrose.
source: To independently confirm the response of the IR60b neuron to sucrose, we drove the GCaMP6s reporter with a different driver, IR94f-GAL4, which is coexpressed in the same neuron (Figure 2J–L). Again, we found an increase in fluorescence, with comparable dynamics (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sucrose acts via the IR60b receptor to activate the IR60b neuron.
source: The simplest interpretation of these imaging results is that sucrose acts via the IR60b receptor to activate the IR60b neuron, which in turn activates a circuit that inhibits feeding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined behavioral and imaging data.

claim: The IR60b neuron activates a circuit that inhibits feeding.
source: The simplest interpretation of these imaging results is that sucrose acts via the IR60b receptor to activate the IR60b neuron, which in turn activates a circuit that inhibits feeding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined behavioral and imaging data.

claim: The IR60b receptor limits sucrose consumption in freely moving flies under conditions comparable to natural foraging and feeding.
source: The simplest interpretation of these results is that the IR60b receptor is required not only to prevent overconsumption of sucrose in the pharyngeal pumping paradigm but also in freely moving flies under conditions more comparable to natural foraging and feeding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FLIC assay data.

claim: IR60b is a sucrose receptor or co-receptor.
source: The simplest interpretation of our results is that IR60b is a sucrose receptor or co-receptor.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined behavioral and imaging data.

claim: At high concentrations, glucose may bind to a site that has evolved to bind sucrose.
source: Sucrose is a dissaccharide composed of the monosaccharides glucose and fructose, and it is possible that at high concentrations glucose may bind to a site that has evolved to bind sucrose.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of glucose response.

claim: The high specificity of the IR60b phenotype argues against a role for the IR60b receptor in signaling osmolarity, viscosity, or mechanosensory stimulation.
source: We note that the high specificity of the IR60b phenotype argues against a role for the IR60b receptor in signaling osmolarity, viscosity, or mechanosensory stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference from the specificity of the behavioral phenotype.

claim: The IR60b neuron does not alone dictate the level of consumption.
source: We note that both loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments suggest that the IR60b neuron does not alone dictate the level of consumption.
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral data showing partial effects.

claim: The IR60b neuron acts as a brake to temper the activity of other neurons that promote feeding.
source: Rather, the IR60b neuron appears to act as a brake, to temper the activity of other neurons that promote feeding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data.

claim: The IR60b neuron may provide a mechanism for moderating the rate of sucrose intake and thereby helping to maintain homeostasis.
source: The IR60b neuron may provide a mechanism for moderating the rate of sucrose intake and thereby helping to maintain homeostasis.
evidence: This is speculation about the physiological function of the IR60b neuron.

claim: A fast-acting inhibition from peripheral taste receptors could prevent a rapid influx of sugar into the system.
source: A fast-acting inhibition could prevent a rapid influx of sugar into the system.
evidence: This is speculation about the advantage of peripheral inhibition.

claim: By tempering the dynamics of sugar intake, the circuit could prevent the system from quickly moving far from equilibrium and requiring major metabolic costs to restore.
source: By tempering the dynamics of sugar intake, the circuit could prevent the system from quickly moving far from equilibrium and requiring major metabolic costs to restore.
evidence: This is speculation about the metabolic advantage of the IR60b circuit.

claim: Peripheral osmolarity detectors may be responsible in part for the cessation of water drinking before systemic osmolarity levels are affected in mammals.
source: A similar mechanism could exist in mammals to limit water ingestion: peripheral osmolarity detectors may be responsible in part for the cessation of water drinking before systemic osmolarity levels are affected (Bourque, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bourque, 2008.

claim: Dual control mechanisms may allow the feeding system to be fine-tuned more precisely.
source: Dual control may allow the system to be fine-tuned more precisely.
evidence: This is speculation about the advantage of dual control.

claim: Changes in the internal state of the fly could affect feeding by modulation of both positive and negative control mechanisms.
source: For example, changes in the internal state of the fly could in principle affect feeding by modulation of both positive and negative control mechanisms.
evidence: This is speculation about how internal state could modulate feeding.

claim: Satiety negatively modulates Gr43a neurons.
source: For example, satiety negatively modulates Gr43a neurons, and it will be interesting to determine whether satiety positively modulates IR60b neurons.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge for comparison.

claim: As fruits ripen, sucrose levels decline and the levels of other sugars increase in many cases.
source: As fruits ripen, sucrose levels decline and the levels of other sugars increase in many cases (Akazawa and Okamoto, 1980; Chareoansiri and Kongkachuichai, 2009; Hardy, 1967; Schwieterman et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster prefers feeding on fruits that are at advanced stages of ripening.
source: Drosophila melanogaster prefers feeding on fruits that are at advanced stages of ripening.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: A circuit that inhibits feeding on sources rich in sucrose might tend to favor feeding on food sources with low sucrose concentrations.
source: Perhaps a circuit that inhibits feeding on sources rich in sucrose might tend to favor feeding on food sources with low sucrose concentrations.
evidence: This is speculation about the ecological function of the IR60b circuit.

claim: The central projections of the IR60b neuron differ from those of other pharyngeal neurons.
source: We note finally that the central projections of the IR60b neuron differ from those of other pharyngeal neurons.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about neuroanatomy.

claim: GAL4 drivers representing receptors of the IR20a clade label projections in the dorsoanterior subesophageal zone.
source: GAL4 drivers representing receptors of the IR20a clade label projections in the dorsoanterior subesophageal zone (Koh et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Koh et al., 2014.

claim: IR60b and IR94f drivers show no projections toward the midline, differing from other IR20a clade drivers.
source: However, drivers of IR60b and IR94f, which are coexpressed (Figure 2P), differ from the others in that they show no projections toward the midline (Koh et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Koh et al., 2014.

claim: The IR60b driver differs from Gr-GAL4 drivers expressed in the pharynx in its projection pattern.
source: In this respect, the IR60b driver also differs from Gr-GAL4 drivers expressed in the pharynx (Kwon et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kwon et al., 2014.

claim: In both flies and mammals, NaCl has a negative valence with some taste neurons and a positive valence with others.
source: In both flies and mammals, NaCl has a negative valence with some taste neurons (Amrein and Thorne, 2005; Hiroi et al., 2004), and a positive valence with others (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Amrein and Thorne, 2005, Hiroi et al., 2004, and Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: NaCl acts on different taste neurons at different concentrations in flies and mammals.
source: However, NaCl acts on these different neurons at different concentrations, whereas sucrose acts on the IR60b and Gr43a neurons at the same concentration.
evidence: This is stated as a contrast to the sucrose case.

claim: Overconsumption of sugar is a major cause of a rapidly expanding worldwide obesity epidemic in humans.
source: Overconsumption of sugar is a major cause of a rapidly expanding worldwide obesity epidemic in humans (WHO, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to WHO, 2011.
